g11-mathematics-um4-t1.overview: The determinant of a 2×2 matrix: det = ad − bc. Its meaning (area scale factor / invertibility test), its geometry (the parallelogram), and quick computation.
objectives: Compute det[a b; c d] = ad − bc
Connect det = 0 with singularity (no inverse)
Interpret |det| as the area scale factor
Use the determinant to classify 2×2 systems
Handle sign and orientation notes
g11-mathematics-um4-t1.simple: Every square matrix carries a single number: its determinant. For 2×2: det [a b; c d] = ad − bc — 'down the main diagonal, minus up the other'. Example: [3 1; 2 4] → 3·4 − 1·2 = 10. Why care? Three jobs. (1) Invertibility: A has an inverse iff det ≠ 0 — the 2×2 inverse divides by ad − bc, so zero there = no inverse. [1 2; 2 4]: det = 0 — singular (rows proportional). (2) Systems: for Ax = b with 2×2 A, det ≠ 0 guarantees exactly one solution; det = 0 means none or infinitely many. (3) Geometry: |det| is the AREA of the parallelogram spanned by the two row (or column) vectors — [3 1; 2 4] spans area 10; and as a scale factor: multiplying a shape by A multiplies its area by |det A| (the shear had det 1 → area preserved; scaling by 2 has det 4 → area ×4). The sign carries orientation: det > 0 keeps the plane's handedness, det < 0 flips it (reflections have negative determinant). Compute in seconds; interpret for the marks.
g11-mathematics-um4-t1.detailed:
Formula & conventions. det A = |a b; c d| = ad − bc (vertical bars = determinant of the matrix). Note det is a NUMBER, not a matrix; det ≠ 'modulus' — it can be negative. Common slips: order (ad − bc, not ac − bd) and signs with negative entries: [−2 3; 1 −4] → (−2)(−4) − (3)(1) = 8 − 3 = 5.

Invertibility & systems. The 2×2 inverse A⁻¹ = [d −b; −c a]/(ad − bc) exists exactly when ad − bc ≠ 0. For the system ax+by=e, cx+dy=f: det = ad − bc; det ≠ 0 → unique solution (Cramer: x = (ed − bf)/det, y = (af − ec)/det — t6); det = 0 → lines parallel or coincident (check consistency by elimination). Discriminating 2×2 systems by determinant is faster than full elimination.

Geometry. Rows (a,b) and (c,d) as vectors from the origin span a parallelogram; its area = |ad − bc| (shoelace formula in disguise). det = 0 ⇔ vectors collinear ⇔ zero-area parallelogram ⇔ the matrix collapses the plane (singular). Under the linear map A, the unit square maps to that parallelogram — hence 'area scale factor'. Orientation: the ordered pair of image vectors is counterclockwise (positive det) or clockwise (negative) — reflections give det = −1. Triangle area: half the parallelogram — vertices (x₁,y₁)… via the 3×3 determinant (t7's application).

g11-mathematics-um4-t2.overview: Minors and cofactors: the building blocks of 3×3 determinants and inverses. The minor Mᵢⱼ deletes row i, column j; the cofactor Cᵢⱼ adds the checkerboard sign (−1)^(i+j).
objectives: Compute minors Mᵢⱼ of 3×3 matrices
Apply the sign checkerboard for cofactors Cᵢⱼ
Expand a determinant along any row/column
Build the cofactor matrix and adjugate (transpose)
Use minors in the area-of-triangle formula
g11-mathematics-um4-t2.simple: To handle 3×3 determinants, break them into 2×2s. The MINOR Mᵢⱼ of entry aᵢⱼ: delete row i and column j — what remains is a 2×2 whose determinant is the minor. The COFACTOR: same thing with a sign — Cᵢⱼ = (−1)^(i+j)·Mᵢⱼ. The signs form a checkerboard: + − + / − + − / + − + (position (1,1) starts +). Example A = [1 2; 3 4] extended... take 3×3: [2 1 0; 1 3 1; 0 1 2]. Minor M₁₁ = det[3 1; 1 2] = 5; C₁₁ = +5. M₁₂ = det[1 1; 0 2] = 2; C₁₂ = −2 (checkerboard flips it). Laplace expansion: det A = a₁₁C₁₁ + a₁₂C₁₂ + a₁₃C₁₃ (pick any row or column — the answer is the same; choose the one with zeros to do less work). The adjugate adj(A): the matrix of cofactors, TRANSPOSED — it feeds the inverse formula A⁻¹ = adj(A)/det(A) (t5). Minors also measure: the triangle with vertices in the plane uses a 3×3 determinant built from minors.
g11-mathematics-um4-t2.detailed:
Mechanics. For 3×3 A: Mᵢⱼ = determinant of the 2×2 left after deleting row i and column j (9 minors). Cᵢⱼ = (−1)^(i+j) Mᵢⱼ — the sign depends only on POSITION: + on (1,1),(1,3),(2,2),(3,1),(3,3); − on the others. The cofactor matrix C = [Cᵢⱼ]; the adjugate adj A = Cᵀ (swap across the diagonal — students forget the transpose constantly).

Laplace expansion. det A = Σⱼ aᵢⱼCᵢⱼ for ANY fixed row i (or Σᵢ aᵢⱼCᵢⱼ for any column j) — all six expansions agree. Strategy: expand along the row/column with the most zeros (each zero kills a 2×2). Worked: [2 1 0; 1 3 1; 0 1 2] along row 1: 2·C₁₁ + 1·C₁₂ + 0 = 2(6−1) − 1(2−0) = 10 − 2 = 8.

Why the transpose in adjugate. The identity A·adj(A) = det(A)·I pairs each row of A with cofactors from the CORRESPONDING COLUMN positions — the cross-cancellation (row i with cofactors of row j ≠ i gives 0) requires the transpose to align indices. This identity is exactly what makes adj/det the inverse (t5).

Pattern recognition. For 2×2, minors are single entries (M₁₁ = d) — the 2×2 inverse formula [d −b; −c a]/det IS the adjugate rule in miniature: cofactor matrix of [a b; c d] is [d −c; −b a], transposed = [d −b; −c a]. The checkerboard's − on off-diagonals explains the sign flip.

g11-mathematics-um4-t3.overview: 3×3 determinants: the diagonal (Sarrus) rule, cofactor expansion, and the same interpretation as 2×2 — volume scale factor and invertibility test.
objectives: Compute 3×3 determinants by Sarrus' rule
Compute by cofactor (Laplace) expansion
Choose the efficient method per matrix
Interpret det as volume scale / singularity test
Avoid the classic sign and copy errors
g11-mathematics-um4-t3.simple: Two reliable ways to get a 3×3 determinant. METHOD 1 — Sarrus (diagonals): write the first two columns again beside the matrix; sum the three down-right diagonals, subtract the three down-left diagonals. For [a b c; d e f; g h i]: det = aei + bfg + cdh − ceg − bdi − afh. METHOD 2 — cofactor expansion (previous topic): pick the zeriest row/column, det = Σ entries × cofactors. Example: [2 1 0; 1 3 1; 0 1 2]: along row 1 → 2(6−1) − 1(2−0) + 0 = 10 − 2 = 8. Both give the same number — Sarrus is fast for full 3×3s; expansion wins when zeros exist (and generalizes to any size). Meaning, same as 2×2: det ≠ 0 ⇔ invertible ⇔ unique solutions; |det| = the VOLUME scale factor (the parallelepiped spanned by the three row vectors); det = 0 ⇔ the three vectors are coplanar (volumeless). Triangles/areas and tetrahedra/volumes come out as determinant applications (t7).
g11-mathematics-um4-t3.detailed:
Sarrus mechanics. Copy columns 1–2 to the right; down-right products (aei, bfg, cdh) positive; down-left (ceg, afh... careful: the three up-right diagonals ceg, bdi, afh) subtracted. Sarrus works ONLY for 3×3 — it fails for 2×2 (no) and 4×4 (wrong). The pattern is the even/odd permutation rule of the general determinant: 6 terms = 3! permutations, sign by parity.

Expansion strategy. Choose the line with most zeros; each nonzero entry costs one 2×2. With one zero: 2 minors; with two: 1 minor. Row-reduce FIRST if the matrix came from a system (t4's elimination preserves det up to known factors: swap flips sign, scale multiplies, add-multiple preserves — see t4's properties in t4... t4's properties in next topic). Combined: reduce to triangular, then det = diagonal product — the fastest route for big/dense matrices.

Geometry & algebra checks. det [rows u; v; w] = u · (v × w) — the scalar triple product: volume of the parallelepiped, sign by handedness of (u,v,w). Coplanar rows ⇔ det 0. Quick sanity: identity det 1; a matrix with a zero row det 0; triangular det = diagonal product (Sarrus confirms: [2 1 0; 0 3 1; 0 0 4] → 24).

Error patterns. Sign drift in expansion (the checkerboard applies to the POSITION, not the minor's own sign); copying the wrong 2×2 after deletion (visualize the cross-out); Sarrus diagonal misreading (draw the lines). Verify with a second method when the answer matters — determinants are the 'cheap to state, easy to slip' computation.

g11-mathematics-um4-t4.overview: Determinant properties: det(AB) = det A·det B, det(Aᵀ) = det A, det(A⁻¹) = 1/det A, row-operation effects (swap flips, scale multiplies, add-multiple preserves), triangular shortcut — the toolkit that makes determinant work elegant.
objectives: Apply det(AB) = det A det B and its powers

g11-mathematics-um4-t4.simple: You don't always compute — sometimes you reason. THE RULES: (1) det(AB) = (det A)(det B) — determinant of a product is the product of determinants (so det A² = (det A)², det(kA) = kⁿ det A for n×n — every row scaled by k). (2) det(Aᵀ) = det A — transposing changes nothing. (3) If A is invertible, det(A⁻¹) = 1/det A — from AA⁻¹ = I: (det A)(det A⁻¹) = 1. (4) Row operations: SWAP two rows → det flips sign; MULTIPLY a row by k → det ×k; ADD a multiple of one row to another → det UNCHANGED. (5) Triangular → diagonal product. Use them: 'det A = 3, find det(A²Bᵀ)' → 3²·det B. 'Show det A = 0 if A² = A and A ≠ I' → (det A)² = det A → 0 or 1... plus more. 'A row is the sum of two others' → add-multiple ops zero it → det 0. Properties turn 10-minute expansions into 30-second deductions — and they're the exam's favorite 'without expanding' questions.
g11-mathematics-um4-t4.detailed:
Product rule. det(AB) = det A·det B — proof sketch: elementary matrices (each row op scales det predictably) and A = product of elementaries × (triangular). Consequences: det Aⁿ = (det A)ⁿ; det(kA) = kⁿ det A (n rows each scaled); singular detection: det(AB) = 0 if either factor singular; area/volume composition: scale factors multiply (why det is THE scale factor).

Transpose & inverse. det Aᵀ = det A (expansion along rows = expansion of Aᵀ along columns). From AA⁻¹ = I: det A·det A⁻¹ = det I = 1 — so det A ≠ 0 required (invertible ⇔ det ≠ 0, the equivalence in both directions).

Row-operation accounting. Swap: sign flip (orientation reversal). Row ×k: det ×k (scale one direction). Rᵢ + kRⱼ: unchanged (shear — volume-preserving). Strategy for big determinants: eliminate to triangular using only type-3 ops (+ maybe swaps tracked), then diagonal product — usually far fewer arithmetic steps than expansion.

Deduction patterns. Aᵀ = −A (skew, odd n): det A = det(−Aᵀ) = (−1)ⁿ det A = −det A → det = 0. A² = I: (det A)² = 1 → ±1. Rows sum to zero vector: add all other rows to one → zero row → det 0. Orthogonal matrices (AᵀA = I): (det A)² = 1 → det = ±1 (rotations +1, reflections −1). These 'without computing' arguments are the property questions' core.

g11-mathematics-um4-t5.overview: Inverses of 2×2 and 3×3 matrices via the adjugate formula A⁻¹ = adj(A)/det(A) — minors, cofactors, transpose, and the division — plus the invertibility condition det ≠ 0.
objectives: State A⁻¹ = adj(A)/det(A) and its requirement det ≠ 0

g11-mathematics-um4-t5.simple: The adjugate formula: A⁻¹ = adj(A) / det(A) — the adjugate is the transposed cofactor matrix, and the division is by the single number det A (which is why det ≠ 0 is required — you can't divide by zero; singular confirmed). 2×2 shortcut (the formula in miniature): [a b; c d]⁻¹ = [d −b; −c a]/(ad − bc) — swap the diagonal, negate the off-diagonal, divide by det. 3×3 recipe: (1) det A (Sarrus/expansion); if 0, STOP — no inverse; (2) all 9 cofactors (checkerboard!); (3) transpose the cofactor matrix → adj; (4) divide every entry by det. Worked for A = [2 1 0; 1 3 1; 0 1 2] (det 8 from t3): cofactors C₁₁ = 5, C₁₂ = −2, C₁₃ = 1, C₂₁ = −2, C₂₂ = 4, C₂₃ = −2, C₃₁ = 1, C₃₂ = −2, C₃₃ = 5 → adj = Cᵀ = [5 −2 1; −2 4 −2; 1 −2 5] → A⁻¹ = ⅛ of that. Verify: AA⁻¹ = I. Which method? Adjugate shows structure (and feeds Cramer's rule); row-reduction [A|I] is usually faster for 3×3 and much faster for bigger — know both, use either.
g11-mathematics-um4-t5.detailed:
Why the formula works. A·adj(A) = det(A)·I: entry (i,j) of the product = Σₖ aᵢₖ·Cⱼₖ — when i = j it's the expansion of det A along row i; when i ≠ j it's the expansion of a matrix with row j duplicated by row i → 0 (the duplicate-row determinant property). Divide by det A (≠ 0) → A⁻¹. The same identity gives det(A⁻¹) = 1/det A immediately.

2×2 worked. A = [3 5; 1 2]: det = 6 − 5 = 1 → A⁻¹ = [2 −5; −1 3]/1 — det 1 matrices have integer inverses (unimodular — the cryptography-friendly kind). Check: [3 5;1 2][2 −5;−1 3] = [6−5, −15+15; 2−2, −5+6] = I ✓.

3×3 workflow discipline. Compute det first (cheapest kill of the whole task if 0). Cofactors in a 3×3 grid, applying the checkerboard as you write (not after). Transpose LAST (adj = Cᵀ). Divide by det at the END (keep fractions factored: (1/det)·adj is cleaner than distributing). Verify one row-column pair of AA⁻¹ = I (full check if time). Symmetry shortcut: for symmetric A, the cofactor matrix is already symmetric → adj = C (no visible change) — the example above shows it.

Method comparison. Adjugate: 10 determinants (det + 9 minors) — good for theory, Cramer, and small matrices with structure. Row-reduction: ~n³/2 ops — better for 3×3+ numerically. Both must agree — a mismatch is an arithmetic error, usually a checkerboard sign.

g11-mathematics-um4-t6.simple: Cramer's rule: each unknown is a ratio of determinants. For Ax = b, x = det(Aₓ)/det(A), y = det(A_y)/det(A), … where Aₓ is A with column 1 swapped for the constants b (column 2 for y, etc.). 2×2 example: 2x + y = 5, x − y = 1 → det A = −3; Aₓ = [5 1; 1 −1] → det = −6 → x = −6/−3 = 2; A_y = [2 5; 1 1] → det = −3 → y = 1. Same answer as elimination — different road. The catch: det A = 0 kills the rule (division by zero) — then fall back to elimination to distinguish 'none' from 'infinitely many'. Cost: n+1 determinants for n unknowns — fine for 2×2/3×3 by hand, wasteful for big systems (elimination wins). Why learn it: exam staple, and the formula PROVES when solutions exist (det ≠ 0) and shows how each variable responds to each constant (the sensitivity/economics reading: ∂xᵢ/∂bⱼ = cofactor ratio).
g11-mathematics-um4-t6.detailed:
Derivation (one line). x = A⁻¹b = adj(A)b/det A; row i of adj(A)·b = Σⱼ Cⱼᵢbⱼ = the expansion of det(A with column i replaced by b) — hence xᵢ = det(Aᵢ)/det A. The adjugate formula IS Cramer's rule in matrix clothing.

Mechanics. Build Aᵢ carefully: replace the ENTIRE column i with b, keep all other columns from A. For 3×3: four determinants (det A + three Aᵢ) — use the zeriest expansion each time. Signs: a negative det ratio is fine (x = −2 is a valid answer; context decides physical acceptability).

The singular case. det A = 0: Cramer fails; the system has none or infinitely many — elimination on [A|b] distinguishes ([0 0|c] row vs [0 0|0]). A special sub-case: det A = 0 AND all det Aᵢ = 0 → dependent (∞ many); det A = 0 with some Aᵢ ≠ 0 → inconsistent.

Efficiency & use-cases. Cramer: (n+1)·O(n!) naive or O(n⁴) with good det computation — elimination: O(n³). For 2×2/3×3 hand work Cramer is clean and parallel (each variable independent — nice for theory and for 'solve for x only' questions). Applications: sensitivity analysis (comparative statics in economics — ∂x/∂b from the cofactor ratio), electrical networks solving one current, and proofs (integer/unimodular systems keep integer solutions — Cramer shows why: det ±1 divides everything).

workedExamples.problem: For unimodular A (det = ±1) with integer b, why are solutions integers?
workedExamples.substitution: xᵢ = det(Aᵢ)/±1 — det(Aᵢ) is an integer (integer entries) — division by ±1 preserves integrality
workedExamples.answer: Cramer proves it: ±1 divides every integer determinant

commonMistakes: Replacing a ROW with b — Cramer replaces COLUMNS (one per variable)
Forgetting which column goes with which variable (x = column 1, y = column 2…)
Applying Cramer when det A = 0 — the rule is silent there; switch methods
Computing det Aᵢ with the original column still in place — the replaced column must be b
Sign errors in 3×3 numerators — expand along the zeriest line
Assuming Cramer is 'better' — for big systems it's dramatically slower
applications: Exam technique: 'find x only' — one numerator determinant, no full solve
Economics: comparative statics — how equilibrium x shifts with demand constant b
Electrical engineering: solving one branch current in small networks
Number theory: unimodular systems preserve integer solutions
g11-mathematics-um4-t6.summary: Cramer's rule: xᵢ = det(Aᵢ)/det(A), Aᵢ = A with column i replaced by the constants b. It's the adjugate inverse applied to b — hence it fails exactly when det A = 0 (then elimination decides none-vs-infinite). For 2×2/3×3 hand work it's clean and variable-by-variable; for large systems elimination wins on speed. Its theory gifts: existence (det ≠ 0), sensitivity (cofactor ratios), and integer-preservation for unimodular matrices.

g11-mathematics-um4-t7.overview: Determinants applied: areas of triangles and parallelograms (shoelace), volumes, collinearity/coplanarity tests, and the geometry of linear systems — the 'what is a determinant FOR' topic.
objectives: Compute triangle area via the 3×3 determinant
Test collinearity of three points with determinants
Compute parallelogram/parallelepiped areas and volumes
Apply determinants to unknown-coordinate problems
Connect det sign to orientation
g11-mathematics-um4-t7.simple: Determinants are geometry machines. TRIANGLE AREA from vertices (x₁,y₁), (x₂,y₂), (x₃,y₃): Area = ½|det [x₁ y₁ 1; x₂ y₂ 1; x₃ y₃ 1]| — the 'shoelace' determinant. Example: (0,0), (4,0), (1,3): det = 0(0−3) − 0(...) + 1(12 − 0)... expand row 1: +1·det[4 0; 1 3] = 12 → area 6. COLLINEARITY: three points are on one line iff that determinant = 0 (zero-area triangle) — the fastest collinearity test. PARALLELOGRAM: |det| of the two edge vectors as rows (2×2) — no ½. PARALLELEPIPED: |det| of three edge vectors (3×3) — volume. Unknown coordinates: 'find k so that (1,2), (3,k), (5,6) are collinear' → set the determinant to 0 → solve. Orientation: positive determinant = counterclockwise vertex order; negative = clockwise — useful in computer graphics (back-face culling). The unifying idea: determinant = signed volume, and zero volume = degeneracy (collinear/coplanar/singular). Every geometry question about areas, alignment or flatness is a determinant in disguise.
g11-mathematics-um4-t7.detailed:
Shoelace & triangle. The 3×3 with column of 1s computes twice the signed area (the 1s anchor the affine positions); absolute value + ½ gives area. The vertex-order sign: counterclockwise → positive. For polygons: sum of triangle determinants (the classic shoelace sum Σ(xᵢyᵢ₊₁ − xᵢ₊₁yᵢ)/2 — pairwise determinants).

Collinearity test. det [x₁ y₁ 1; x₂ y₂ 1; x₃ y₃ 1] = 0 ⇔ points collinear ⇔ one point is an affine combination of the other two ⇔ the 'triangle' is flat. Exam pattern: find k from a zero determinant — linear equation in k.

Volumes. Parallelepiped edges u, v, w: V = |det[u; v; w]| (scalar triple product u·(v×w)); tetrahedron = V/6. Coplanarity of four points: the three difference vectors give det 0. These are the 3D upgrades of the area tests.

Systems geometry. For 2 lines a₁x+b₁y = c₁, a₂x+b₂y = c₂: det of coefficients ≠ 0 ⇔ not parallel ⇔ intersection exists (Cramer gives it); det = 0 ⇔ parallel/coincident. The determinant is the algebraic shadow of the geometric 'do they meet?' question. Unimodular lattices (det ±1) tile the plane without distortion — the crystallographic hook.

keyTerms.def: polygon area from vertex determinant sums

commonMistakes: Forgetting the ½ for triangles (the determinant gives DOUBLE the area)
Forgetting the column of 1s in the triangle determinant
Dropping the absolute value — area is positive; the sign is orientation
Using the parallelogram formula for a triangle without halving
Tetrahedron volume as det instead of det/6
Testing collinearity with slopes (breaks for vertical lines) — the determinant never breaks
applications: Surveying & GIS: land-plot areas from coordinate lists (shoelace)
Computer graphics: back-face culling via determinant sign
Robotics: workspace volumes and Jacobian determinants
Physics: phase-space volumes (Liouville), triple products in torque
Ethiopian land administration: parcel areas from boundary coordinates
g11-mathematics-um4-t7.summary: Determinants measure signed volume: triangle area = ½|3×3 determinant with a 1-column|, parallelogram = |2×2|, parallelepiped = |3×3|, tetrahedron = /6. Zero determinant = degeneracy: collinear points, coplanar vectors, singular systems — the universal alignment test. The sign records orientation (CCW vs CW). Every 'find k so points line up' problem is one linear equation from one determinant.
